query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperature in chloride‐containing environments, cyclic mechanical wear disrupts the thermally formed protective oxide layers on the eutectic HEA, repeatedly exposing the inherently galvanic phase boundaries between the FCC (or L12) and BCC (or B2) regions. This exposure initiates localized corrosion at these interfaces, which in turn further destabilizes the oxide layer, thus accelerating overall degradation by coupling wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a fine lamellar microstructure with alternating FCC (or L12) and BCC (or B2) phases.
generation.intervention: Subjecting identical samples to a controlled cyclic sliding wear load under a corrosive atmosphere (e.g., chloride-containing environment) at an elevated temperature (e.g., 800–900 °C), while comparing to samples exposed to wear-only and corrosion-only conditions.
generation.conditions: High temperature (800–900 °C) in an atmospherical environment with a controlled chloride (NaCl) concentration; cyclic sliding wear at constant load and prescribed sliding speed; testing durations sufficient to observe oxide formation and disruption cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity (or breakdown) of the protective oxide film that forms during high temperature exposure and its subsequent mechanical spallation at the phase boundaries of the eutectic lamellae.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature promotes the formation of a protective oxide film, which temporarily reduces wear and corrosion. However, cyclic mechanical stress from wear causes spallation or disruption of this film. The mechanically exposed phase boundaries—with distinct electrochemical potentials due to compositional differences—act as microgalvanic cells. Repeated exposure leads to localized corrosion that undermines both the protective film and the underlying structural integrity, resulting in accelerated coupled degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the combined wear-corrosion conditions, the total degradation (mass loss or pit depth) will be substantially higher (potentially doubling or more) than under either wear-only or corrosion-only conditions. Individually, wear tracks will show more frequent and larger spallation events and deeper pits at phase boundaries, and electrochemical measurements will indicate faster corrosion kinetics (e.g., lower polarization resistance) relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Samples undergoing only sliding wear in an inert or non-corrosive atmosphere and samples immersed in the chloride environment without mechanical wear.
generation.boundary: Results are expected to hold for multi-phase eutectic HEAs with similar lamellar microstructures under high-temperature (800–900 °C) conditions and in chloride-containing atmospheres; deviations in microstructural scale or changes in environmental aggressiveness might alter the interplay between oxide stability and galvanic coupling.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on (1) findings from PMC12156342::web::036::3_2_mechanical_properties regarding the formation and cyclic spallation of protective oxide films under wear, and (2) observations from PMC9319277::web::022::3_4_corrosion_observation that eutectic HEAs exhibit localized pitting likely due to galvanic coupling at phase boundaries. The new element is the explicit coupling mechanism linking mechanical disruption of the oxide to accelerated galvanic corrosion, which has not been directly tested in an integrated study for eutectic HEAs under simultaneous high-temperature wear and corrosion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of identical multi-phase eutectic HEA samples. Subject one set to cyclic sliding wear in a non-corrosive atmosphere (e.g., dry inert gas), a second set to static immersion in the chloride-containing environment at elevated temperature, and a third set to combined cyclic sliding wear in the same chloride-containing environment at the same elevated temperature. Use identical sample geometries, loading conditions, sliding speeds, and exposure times. Employ in-situ monitoring (e.g., high-temperature microscopy and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) to assess oxide film integrity and pit initiation at phase boundaries.
measurements: Mass loss and wear track depth measurements (via laser profilometry)
Microstructural and surface analyses (SEM/EDS mapping of oxide film continuity and pit morphology)
Comparative quantification of spallation events and localized corrosion at phase interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined wear-corrosion samples do not show significantly higher degradation—specifically, if (a) the oxide film remains continuous with minimal mechanical spallation, or (b) the localized corrosion (e.g., pitting depth and density) is not notably higher at the phase boundaries compared to the isolated wear or corrosion tests—then the hypothesis that mechanical oxide disruption exposes galvanic couples driving accelerated degradation would be falsified.

Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.

Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.
